title: Genuino v. De Lima
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that the DOJ Secretary has no inherent power to issue hold departure orders. Only courts have the authority to restrict a person's right to travel. The issuance of a hold departure order during preliminary investigation violates the constitutional right to travel.
doctrine: The right to travel may only be impaired by a court order, not by executive fiat. The DOJ Secretary has no authority to issue hold departure orders. Only a court, in the exercise of its judicial power, may restrict a person's right to travel through the issuance of a hold departure order.
fullText:
ABAD, J.:

The issue is whether the Secretary of Justice has the authority to issue hold departure orders against persons subject to preliminary investigation.

The right to travel is guaranteed by Section 6, Article III of the Constitution. It may only be impaired in the interest of national security, public safety, or public health, as may be provided by law.

The DOJ Secretary's power to issue hold departure orders has no constitutional or statutory basis. The restriction on a person's right to travel may only be imposed by a court of law. A hold departure order constitutes a restraint on liberty that requires judicial sanction.
